title: Northstar: a small customer's migration
disclosure: Synthetic interview — fictional company and speaker

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did your small Northstar deployment migrate?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Our small deployment moved in six weeks because we used only standard connectors.

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: We had twelve users and did not maintain custom integrations. This was one migration, not a representative survey.

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: I cannot estimate how an enterprise deployment would compare.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Can you describe a key preparation task and any uncertainties involved?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: One important preparation task was auditing all user accounts to confirm active status before migration. We handed this list off to the migration team to ensure only current users were included. However, there was uncertainty about whether some dormant accounts might still need access post-migration. To manage this, we flagged uncertain accounts for review but could not fully verify their future use. This meant the migration team had to be ready for potential access adjustments after go-live. The handoff was clear, but the limits of our knowledge created a small risk of delayed access for some users.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did you implement recordkeeping and handle unobservable issues?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: We implemented recordkeeping by maintaining detailed logs of each migration step in a shared document. A practical workaround was using manual entry for some automated steps that lacked full traceability. This allowed us to track progress despite tool limitations. However, we could not observe some backend processes directly, such as data transfer speeds or internal error handling. We relied on system reports but knew these might not capture every anomaly. The workaround ensured continuity, but our view was incomplete, so we planned follow-up checks post-migration to catch any missed issues.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How might a colleague misunderstand your local migration process?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: A colleague might assume our migration process included custom connectors because of our thorough documentation, but we only used standard connectors. I explained that while our process looked detailed, it was streamlined without custom code, which limited complexity. This misunderstanding could lead to overestimating the time or resources needed for similar projects. I clarified that our approach was unique to our small scale and that larger deployments might require different steps. Emphasizing these limits helped set realistic expectations about what our process represented and prevented misapplication of our experience.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Did you face any challenges arranging shared workspaces or labeling storage?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Yes, arranging shared workspaces was tricky because team members used different naming conventions for folders. We handed off a proposed labeling scheme to the team, but some resisted changing habits, causing confusion. Our workaround was to create a simple reference sheet with examples and reminders, distributed via email. Despite this, some folders remained inconsistently labeled, which occasionally slowed file retrieval. The effort helped, but we never fully standardized naming. This was a minor distraction unrelated to the migration itself but affected daily collaboration and required ongoing reminders to maintain some order.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did you manage meeting agendas or shared stationery supplies?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Managing meeting agendas was a minor inconvenience since no one consistently updated the shared calendar. We handed off agenda preparation to a rotating team member, but last-minute changes often disrupted plans. For stationery, the shared cupboard was frequently disorganized, so we assigned a volunteer to restock and label items weekly. The workaround was informal check-ins to remind everyone to return supplies properly. Neither issue impacted the migration but did slow daily operations slightly. The handoffs worked well enough, though we never measured effectiveness, relying on team goodwill to keep things functional.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Can you give an example of passing a task to a colleague while noting observation limits?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: I passed the responsibility for final user account verification to a colleague after completing initial checks. I explained that while I reviewed active accounts, I could not fully confirm some users’ ongoing needs due to limited access to department plans. The colleague accepted the task but was aware that some accounts might require later adjustment. This handoff included a note about my observation limits and the potential need for follow-up. It ensured continuity but acknowledged that my knowledge was incomplete, so the colleague had to monitor and adapt as necessary during the migration’s final phase.
